The sample contains daily adjusted market prices from 2015 through the end of
2025. The portfolio combines equities, bonds and gold to create a simple
multi-asset allocation suitable for illustrating portfolio-level downside risk.

## Methodology

```{=html}
<div class="method-grid">
  <div class="method-card">
    <span>01</span>
    <h3>Market Data</h3>
    <p>Download adjusted daily prices for SPY, IEF and GLD using <code>yfinance</code>.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>02</span>
    <h3>Portfolio Returns</h3>
    <p>Convert prices to log returns and aggregate them using fixed portfolio weights.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>03</span>
    <h3>Historical Risk</h3>
    <p>Estimate 99% Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk from realized returns.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>04</span>
    <h3>Monte Carlo</h3>
    <p>Generate 10,000 daily return scenarios from the historical mean and volatility.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

Daily log returns are calculated as

$$
r_t = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right).
$$

The portfolio return is then obtained from the weighted asset returns. Historical
VaR identifies the loss threshold exceeded by roughly the worst 1% of historical
observations. CVaR (Expected Shortfall) measures the average loss beyond that
threshold.

The Monte Carlo component intentionally uses a simple normal-distribution
assumption. It is therefore a **baseline model**, not a claim that financial
returns are normally distributed.

## Key Results

```{=html}
<div class="result-grid">
  <div class="result-card">
    <span class="result-label">HISTORICAL VaR</span>
    <strong>1.65%</strong>
    <small>99% confidence</small>
  </div>

  <div class="result-card featured-result">
    <span class="result-label">HISTORICAL CVaR</span>
    <strong>2.52%</strong>
    <small>99% expected shortfall</small>
  </div>

  <div class="result-card">
    <span class="result-label">MONTE CARLO VaR</span>
    <strong>1.37%</strong>
    <small>10,000 simulations</small>
  </div>

  <div class="result-card">
    <span class="result-label">MONTE CARLO CVaR</span>
    <strong>1.60%</strong>
    <small>99% expected shortfall</small>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="case-insight">
  <span class="case-label">MAIN TAKEAWAY</span>
  <p>
    Historical tail losses are larger than those generated by the normal Monte
    Carlo baseline. The difference is especially visible in CVaR:
    <strong>2.52%</strong> historically versus <strong>1.60%</strong> in simulation.
  </p>
</div>
```

The portfolio also produced an annualized historical return of approximately
**9.01%** with annualized volatility of **9.64%**. The largest daily loss in the
sample was approximately **5.83%**.

the different long-run paths of equities, bonds and gold easier to compare.

## Conclusion

The project demonstrates a transparent workflow for moving from market prices to
portfolio returns, historical tail-risk estimation and Monte Carlo stress
testing.

The key comparison is between **realized historical losses** and a
**normal-distribution simulation baseline**. Historical VaR and especially
historical CVaR are larger, indicating that the simple parametric model does not
fully reproduce the severity of downside observations present in the historical
sample.

A natural next step would be to extend the framework with fat-tailed
distributions, time-varying volatility, dynamic correlations, multi-day risk
horizons and explicit historical crisis scenarios.
